title: Nicotine and alcohol dependence drugs: reward, craving and acetaldehyde
ariaLabel: Schematic of three targets in nicotine and alcohol dependence: nicotine receptors that give reward, craving circuits, and the breakdown of alcohol to acetaldehyde. Nicotine replacement and varenicline act at nicotine receptors, acamprosate and naltrexone lower craving, and disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase so acetaldehyde builds up after alcohol.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lipid value is shown or implied.
blockInfo: A drug of the chosen class acting at this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape). Less passes here, with the effects shown at the cholesterol and the LDL receptors.

nodes.label: Nicotine receptors
nodes.info: Nicotine acts on alpha-4 beta-2 receptors in the reward system.

nodes.label: Reward and withdrawal
nodes.info: Reward and withdrawal symptoms from nicotine receptors.

nodes.label: Craving circuits
nodes.info: Glutamate and opioid signalling in craving circuits.

nodes.label: Alcohol breakdown
nodes.info: Alcohol is turned into acetaldehyde, then into acetate.

nodes.label: Urge to use
nodes.info: A teaching score for the urge to smoke or drink. Disulfiram works by making drinking unpleasant rather than lowering the urge, so its effect appears as a lower score here.

edges.label: nicotine receptor
edges.info: Nicotine replacement gives a steady, lower level of nicotine. Varenicline is a partial agonist that gives a modest stimulus and blocks nicotine's full reward, lowering craving and the pleasure of smoking.
More reward and withdrawal raises craving.

edges.label: craving signal
edges.info: Naltrexone blocks opioid receptors, lowering the reward of alcohol. Acamprosate is thought to calm the over-active glutamate (NMDA) system of early abstinence.
More craving raises the urge to use.

edges.label: aldehyde dehydrogenase
edges.info: Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, so drinking causes acetaldehyde to build up with flushing, palpitations and vomiting. It works only as a deterrent in people who want to stay abstinent.
More clearance means no reaction, and so no deterrent.

sources: Where each class acts. Nicotine replacement and varenicline act at nicotine receptors, naltrexone and acamprosate lower craving, and disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Bupropion mechanism, withdrawal management with benzodiazepines, thiamine, opioid and other substance dependence, behavioural support, relapse rates, liver and psychiatric cautions, and doses are left out. Urge to use is drawn as a teaching score. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
